solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Manchester man confused with a sailor

indicators.note: something confused is muddled out of its proper order, so these letters must be rearranged

blocks.note: both words taken letter for letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bewildered Mancunian is mistaken for a sailor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Manchester man' reads as a person from the city, but every letter of it, plus the 'a', is raw material for the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A merchant seaman works aboard a commercial vessel, so he is a sailor in the trading fleet rather than the navy.

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the top one is number one, written NO. I
a tom is a male cat

explanation.surface: Top Cat, the cartoon alley cat, is being put forward for something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top Cat' looks like the cartoon character's name but splits into two pieces; NO. I (number one) is how 'top' is written in crossword shorthand.
explanation.definitionFit: A motion is a formal proposal put to a meeting, a suggestion that something be done, hence a recommendation.

clue.text: Manage to hug educated woman I begin to attract in romantic situation

indicators.note: hugging means wrapping your arms around something, so one piece goes around the other
the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: to run a business is to manage it
from the play and film Educating Rita
taken as written
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A man tries to embrace a learned woman and draw her into a love affair.
explanation.walkthrough: Educating Rita is Willy Russell's play about a hairdresser who studies literature, which is why an educated woman is a fair way to clue the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruritania is the invented Central European kingdom of Anthony Hope's adventure novels, a byword for swashbuckling romantic settings.

clue.text: You and I fly around at the same time

indicators.note: something placed around another surrounds it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: to hover is to fly while staying in one place
you and I together are we

explanation.surface: Two people take off and circle together in unison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At the same time' suggests simultaneity, but here it is the concessive sense, as in 'it is cheap; at the same time, it is ugly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases introduce a contrasting point, meaning nevertheless or yet, so they are interchangeable as sentence connectives.

indicators.note: a thing that conceals keeps something tucked out of sight within itself, so the letters sit inside a word

blocks.note: found in the middle of the word

explanation.surface: Shrewd behaviour hiding the scheming of senior churchmen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cardinals' evokes red-robed clerics, but here it means cardinal numbers, the counting numbers one, two, three and so on.
explanation.definitionFit: Nine is a cardinal number, an ordinary counting number as opposed to an ordinal like ninth, so nines are examples.

indicators.note: Bow is in the East End of London, where Cockney speech famously drops an initial aitch sound

blocks.note: a hen, pronounced without its first letter in Cockney fashion
the tails sit at the rumps of birds

explanation.surface: Someone in an East London pub insists on ordering chicken parson's noses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bow' looks like a ribbon or archery bow but is the East London district within the sound of Bow Bells; Cockneys say 'en for hen.
explanation.definitionFit: If one thing entails another it requires or necessitates it, so entails works as a synonym of demands in that logical sense.

indicators.note: odd here means the odd-numbered positions, first, third and fifth, so only those letters are kept

blocks.note: a mo is a moment, a very short time like a second
letters one, three and five of the boat's name

explanation.surface: A second rowing boat is strangely transformed into a cutter, another kind of vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: A cutter is also a sailing boat, so with 'wherry' (a light rowing boat) the surface stays on the water; the definition is the machine that cuts grass.
explanation.definitionFit: A mower is a machine for cutting grass or crops, so it is literally a cutter, just not the boat the surface suggests.

clue.text: Nero wickedly suffused with desire in the past

indicators.note: acting wickedly is behaving badly and out of line, so the letters are thrown into a new order
something suffused with another is filled through by it, so one piece is placed inside the other

blocks.note: the Roman emperor's name, as raw letters
to long is to desire

explanation.surface: The emperor Nero, once filled with sinful lust, in days gone by.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a history lesson about Nero's vices; the emperor is only four letters to scramble around the yearning.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that happens no longer has stopped and belongs to former times, so the phrase is an adverbial equivalent.

blocks.note: first meaning: to strangle someone by the neck
second meaning: the pedal or lever controlling an engine's fuel flow

explanation.walkthrough: Choke and accelerator are both engine controls, which makes the clue look like a single motoring question; one word is a verb for strangling and also the engine's power control.
explanation.definitionFit: To throttle is to strangle by the windpipe, and an engine's throttle is the valve that the accelerator pedal opens.

clue.text: Restart the drier, or stop trying

blocks.note: first meaning, read literally: toss a damp bath sheet back into the tumble dryer
second meaning: the idiom for giving up

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a whimsical literal reading of the idiom, from the boxing practice of a trainer tossing a towel into the ring to concede.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase comes from boxing, where a corner man concedes a fight on behalf of his fighter, so it means admitting defeat and quitting.

clue.text: Avocets flying in formations of eight

indicators.note: birds in flight scatter and regroup, so these letters move into a different order

blocks.note: the wading birds, taken as raw letters

explanation.surface: Wading birds fly overhead in flocks arranged in groups of eight.
explanation.walkthrough: The birds really do fly in formation in the surface picture; the definition is musical or poetic.
explanation.definitionFit: An octave is a group of eight, whether eight notes of a scale or the eight lines opening a sonnet.

clue.text: About to embrace very small Greek character

indicators.note: an embrace is a hug that encloses someone, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: on means about, as in a book on birds
micro describes something tiny

explanation.surface: Someone is about to hug a tiny Greek person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek character' suggests a person from Greece; it is a letter of the alphabet. The name in fact means 'little O', which makes 'very small' apt.
explanation.definitionFit: Omicron is the fifteenth letter of the Greek alphabet, and a character is a written symbol or letter.

clue.text: Drinker back after ten swilled port

indicators.note: liquid swilled around is sloshed about, so the letters are churned into a new order
going back means travelling the opposite way, so the letters run from end to start
coming after places one piece behind another in the final order

blocks.note: taken as written
a toper is a heavy drinker

explanation.surface: A drinker returns after ten glasses of port knocked back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Port' and 'swilled' sound like the drink, but port is the definition, a harbour town; toper is an old word for a drunkard.
explanation.definitionFit: An entrepot is a trading port where goods are imported and re-exported without duty, so it is a type of harbour.

indicators.note: in a down entry, setting something up raises it so it reads from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: prime means chief or main
the facilities is a euphemism for the toilet, the lav

explanation.surface: The essential utilities have been installed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Facilities' looks like general amenities but is the polite word for the toilet; lav is short for lavatory.
explanation.definitionFit: Primeval means belonging to the earliest ages, so primitive or elemental, which stretches to fundamental or basic.

clue.text: French barman‘s irony driving out Republican

indicators.note: to drive someone out is to expel them, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: satire is mockery through irony
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A French bartender's sarcasm sees off an American politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barman' suggests someone serving drinks; it is a composer, one who writes music in bars. Erik Satie was a French composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Erik Satie wrote piano music such as the Gymnopédies, and music is written in bars, so the composer is whimsically a man of bars.

blocks.note: surface reading: an example of having eaten during a pause
setter's reading: these three letters are what you get when the hot drink is broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone eats, perhaps, during pauses in the working day.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse anagram: the clue shows the result of the rearrangement, and the answer describes how to make it, as a drink whose letters break.
explanation.definitionFit: Short pauses from work for a cup and a biscuit are rest periods, as British offices and building sites call them.

clue.text: Major tech company in the city

blocks.note: major means big or important
Apple is the computer and phone maker

explanation.surface: A large technology firm has offices downtown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Major tech company' reads as one description of a firm; it splits into an adjective and a brand name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Big Apple is the well-known nickname for New York, the archetypal metropolis of the United States.

clue.text: Independent judge is hot under the collar

blocks.note: I is the abbreviation for independent
to rate something is to judge its worth

explanation.surface: A judge with no allegiances is getting angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Judge' looks like a noun for the person on the bench but works as a verb meaning assess.
explanation.definitionFit: Being hot under the collar is an idiom for being angry or flustered, and irate means furious.

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for eastern
states are countries

explanation.surface: Wealth flowing in from nations in the east.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a news story about foreign investment; the pieces are just an abbreviation and a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's estate is the whole of their property and possessions, everything they own of value.

indicators.note: to disperse is to scatter in different directions, so the letters are spread into a new order

blocks.note: the stun-gun verb, taken as raw letters

explanation.surface: Firing a stun gun breaks up a cloud of helium.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark signals that helium is an example of the answer, not a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Helium is one of the noble gases that barely react with anything, which chemists also call inert gases.

clue.text: Giant about to be replaced by a queen

indicators.note: being replaced means swapping one thing out and another in, so one letter is exchanged for another

blocks.note: titanic means gigantic
c is short for circa, about
taken as written

explanation.surface: A giant is about to be dethroned by a queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Giant' looks like a noun but is the adjective; the final C of TITANIC gives way to A. Titania is the fairy queen in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
explanation.definitionFit: Titania is queen of the fairies in Shakespeare's comedy, wife of Oberon, so she is a famous literary queen.

indicators.note: without an end means the final letter is cut off

blocks.note: jerking is pulling sharply, tugging

explanation.surface: Someone keeps pulling at their waistcoat.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a fidgety wearer; the clue is just a synonym with its tail clipped.
explanation.definitionFit: A jerkin is a sleeveless close-fitting jacket, historically leather, much like a waistcoat or vest.

clue.text: Preacher lost out, featuring in Mirror

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or askew, so these letters are put into a different order
to feature in something is to appear inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: to ape is to copy or mirror
taken as raw letters

explanation.surface: A preacher loses out after appearing in the Daily Mirror tabloid.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital M makes 'Mirror' look like the British tabloid newspaper, but it is a verb meaning imitate.
explanation.definitionFit: The apostles were the disciples sent out by Jesus to spread the gospel, so an apostle is a missionary preacher.

indicators.note: without a top means the first letter of a down entry is cut off

blocks.note: to down a drink is to swallow it in one

explanation.surface: Someone drank half-naked, as if possessed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' paints a risqué scene but simply removes the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something possessed belongs to someone, so the past participle owned means the same thing.

blocks.note: surface reading: a reef as a hazard ships must be released from
setter's reading: the four letters are what you get by rearranging a word meaning at liberty

explanation.walkthrough: A reverse anagram: 'reef' is the result, and the answer says how to get it, by setting (arranging) the letters of a word for unconfined.
explanation.definitionFit: To liberate someone is to release them from captivity, which the phrasal verb expresses as letting them go.

blocks.note: first meaning: goes well with, as a colour flatters someone
second meaning: slang for executives in business attire
third meaning: lawsuits brought in court

explanation.walkthrough: Three separate meanings strung together, which reads like a phrase about praising bosses' deeds once the missing apostrophe is imagined.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means flatters or matches, is office slang for executives in business dress, and names legal cases brought to court.

definitions.note: the two printed symbols are examples; the answer names one kind

indicators.note: a rogue element behaves unpredictably and out of line, so the letters go astray into a new order

blocks.note: three words taken as raw letters
to mark something is to notice it

explanation.surface: A rogue state is upset; take heed!
explanation.walkthrough: The double question mark looks like mere bafflement at the end of the clue but is itself the definition, an example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A question mark is a punctuation mark, a symbol used in writing to show structure or tone, so the printed pair are instances of it.

indicators.note: to occupy is to sit within a space, so the letters lie inside the following words

blocks.note: spans the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: The firstborn child lives on a country estate called Bayfield.
explanation.walkthrough: Bayfield sounds like a real stately home, but it is just a carrier for letters running across the word break.
explanation.definitionFit: The eldest child in a family is the one born before all the others, the oldest sibling.

blocks.note: two asses, plural fools
in means fashionable, current

explanation.surface: Idiots holding the current job of winding up a bankrupt company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' suggests electricity (I) or a stream, but here it means in fashion. The plural is two of the same fool.
explanation.definitionFit: To liquidate someone is slang for killing them, so a killer is jokingly a liquidator, hence the question mark.
